chapters.title: Tablet I
paragraphs: Let the one who has tested the heart of all things teach the nation. Let the one who holds all knowledge school all the people; let him pass on his wisdom so that they share it together. Gilgamesh was that master of wisdom, who knew all things. He was the one who uncovered what was hidden. He handed down the tradition of the days before the Flood. He went on a far journey, came back weary and worn by his labour, and carved the whole of his hardship on a tablet of stone.

It was he who built the ramparts of Uruk with its high walls. It was he who set the foundations of Eanna, the sacred temple and holy treasury, firm as bronze, and strengthened its base so that no one could force a way in. He made the threshold that had stood there from ancient times secure, so that no one could force a way into Eanna.
Two-thirds of him is god and one-third of him is man. The shape of his body is beyond the rest, and he has forced others to take whatever he wants.

“He is the one who has taken what belongs to Uruk, and he holds his head high like a wild bull. No weapon can match the shock of his weapons. His companions are driven into his snares, and the heroes of Uruk cower. Gilgamesh leaves no son to his father; his arrogance swells day and night. And yet he is the shepherd of Uruk with its high walls. He is our shepherd, masterful, dominant and cunning. Gilgamesh leaves no girl to her mother, no daughter to a warrior, no wife to her husband.”

The immortals heard the people’s wailing, and the gods of high heaven spoke to Anu, the lord of Uruk: “You have fathered a son who is a tyrant through and through. He holds his head high like a wild bull, and no weapon can match the shock of his weapons. His companions are driven into his snares, and the heroes of Uruk cower. Gilgamesh leaves no son to his father; his arrogance swells day and night. And yet he is the shepherd of Uruk with its high walls. He is their shepherd, masterful, dominant and cunning. Gilgamesh leaves no girl to her mother, no daughter to a warrior, no wife to her husband.”

Anu heard their wailing and called the goddess Aruru: “Aruru, it was you who made the first seed of mankind. Now make a match for him, so that he meets Gilgamesh on the day of his pleasure, so that the two of them fight each other, and Uruk is given rest.”

When the goddess Aruru heard this, she at once formed in her mind the image Anu had asked for. She washed her hands, pinched off some clay and shaped it out on the open plain. There on the plain she made Enkidu, a warrior, as if he had been born and fathered, a double of Ninurta himself. His whole body sprouted hair. He wore his locks like a woman, bound in a band, and his hair grew thick like the bristles on barley. He knew neither people nor country, and he was dressed like Sumuqan, the god of the herds. He grazed on grass with the gazelles, drank his fill with the cattle, and his heart was glad with the animals at the water.

Then a hunter, a trapper, came face to face with this man. He met him one day, a second, a third, at the place where the animals came to drink. When the hunter saw him, his face went dark with terror. He went home to his farmstead with his animals, frightened and shaken, crying out, sick at heart, his face clouded over. There was misery in his belly, and his face looked like the face of a man who has made a long journey.

The hunter opened his mouth and spoke to his father: “Father, a huge man has come down out of the mountains. His strength is the greatest in all the land; it is enormous, like the strength of Anu himself. He roams the hills all the time, always grazing with the herds, always coming down to the water, so I am afraid to go near him. He has filled in the pits I dug with my own hands, pulled up the traps I set, and helped all the animals, the wild beasts of the plain, slip out of my grasp. He will not let me do my work as a hunter.”

His father opened his mouth and answered the hunter: “My son, Gilgamesh lives in Uruk, and no one has ever beaten him. His is the greatest strength in all the land; it is enormous, like the strength of Anu himself. Go, turn your face toward Uruk. When he hears about this monster, he will say: ‘Go, hunter, and take a courtesan with you, a temple girl, as strong as a strong man. When he brings the animals back to the watering place, she will take off her robe and show him her beauty. He will see her and take her in his arms, and from then on the beasts raised alongside him out in his own wild lands will turn their backs on him.’ ”

The hunter listened to his father’s advice and set off at once to find Gilgamesh. He took the road to Uruk, came before Gilgamesh and spoke to him: “A huge man has come down out of the mountains. His strength is the greatest in all the land; it is enormous, like the strength of Anu himself. He roams the hills all the time, always grazing with the herds, always coming down to the water, so I am afraid to go near him. He has filled in the pits I dug with my own hands, pulled up the traps I set, and helped all the animals, the wild beasts of the plain, slip out of my grasp. He will not let me do my work as a hunter.”

Gilgamesh answered the hunter: “Go, my good hunter, and take a courtesan with you, a temple girl. When he brings the animals back to the watering place, she will take off her robe and show him her beauty. He will see her and take her in his arms, and from then on the beasts raised alongside him out in his own wild lands will turn their backs on him.”

The hunter went off and took a courtesan with him, a temple girl. They set out together on the road, and at the end of three days they reached the place they had fixed on. There the hunter and the girl sat down in hiding. One day, two days they sat by the watering place. At last the herds came down to drink their fill. The animals came, glad of heart, to the water, and Enkidu was with them, the one the mountains had brought forth. He grazed on grass with the gazelles, drank his fill with the cattle, and his heart was glad with the animals at the water. And so the courtesan saw him, the great strong man, a creature wild through and through, come out of the depths of the open country!

“That is him, girl! Uncover your beauty, show him your loveliness so that he can take his pleasure in it. Do not be shy in the least. Take his breath away. The moment his eyes fall on you he will come to you. Then loosen your robe so that he can hold you, and work on him with a woman’s arts. Once he has held you to his chest, the animals raised with him in his wild country will turn away from him.”

The girl bared her breasts and showed him her loveliness, and he took his pleasure in her beauty. She was not shy at all. She took his breath away and loosened her robe, and he held her, and she worked on him with a woman’s arts as he held her to his chest. So Enkidu stayed with the courtesan for six days and seven nights, making love to her.

When at last he had had his fill of her charms, he turned back toward his herds. But the gazelles scattered the moment they saw him! The wild beasts of the plain ran from him, from Enkidu himself! Enkidu had lost his innocence. When the herds fled from him his knees gave way, and he could not run as he used to. Yet in this way he had come to his full growth, and his understanding had grown wider.

He came back and sat at the woman’s feet. She studied his face, and as she spoke his ears took in what she said: “You are handsome, Enkidu; you will be godlike. Why wander the open country among the beasts? Come! I will take you to Uruk with its high walls, to the holy temple, the home of Anu and Ishtar, where Gilgamesh lives in the fullness of his power and lords it over men like a wild bull.”

Even as she spoke, her advice won him over, for he felt a longing in himself to find a companion. So he said to the courtesan: “Come then, girl, take me to the holy, sacred temple, the home of Anu and Ishtar, where Gilgamesh lives in the fullness of his power and lords it over men like a wild bull. For I too will call him out. I will challenge him boldly and shout through Uruk, ‘I too am mighty!’ Yes, I will change fate itself. It is the one born in the wild whose strength is greatest! I will please you, and whatever there is to know, I want to know it.”

“Come then, Enkidu, to Uruk with its high walls, where the people dress up splendidly in festival clothes and every day is a celebration, where the eunuch priests clash their cymbals and the dancing girls, giddy with pleasure and full of joy, keep the nobles out of their beds! Enkidu, you will taste the joy of life to the full. I will show you a happy man: Gilgamesh! Look at him, look at his face, see how handsome he is in his manhood! He is full of vigour, his whole body brims with power, and his strength is greater than yours. He never rests, day or night! Enkidu, rein in your pride. Shamash loves Gilgamesh, and Anu, Enlil and Ea have showered him with wisdom.

“Even before you came down from your mountains, Gilgamesh had seen you in Uruk in a dream. Gilgamesh went to his mother to tell her his dream. ‘Mother, I saw a vision in the night. There were stars in the sky, and something like Anu himself fell down on my shoulders. I tried to lift him, but he was too strong for me. I broke his hold, but I could not shake him off. All the while the people of Uruk stood around him, and the craftsmen crowded in.

They pressed on him from behind, the heroes thronged around him, and my own companions kissed his feet. I held him to my chest as I would hold a woman, and then I laid him down at your feet so that you would count him as my equal.’

“She who knows all wisdom answered her lord; she who knows all wisdom answered Gilgamesh: ‘The stars of the sky stand for your companions. The thing like Anu himself that fell on your shoulders, that you tried to lift but that was too strong for you, whose hold you broke but could not shake off, that you laid at my feet so that I would count him your equal, and that you held to your chest like a woman: this is a brave heart, a friend, one who will stand by a comrade. His strength is the greatest in all the land; it is enormous, like the strength of Anu himself. Because you held him to your chest the way you would hold a woman, it is a sign that you are the one he will never abandon. That is the meaning of your dream.’

“He spoke to his mother again: ‘Mother, I saw a second dream. An axe came hurtling down into Uruk with its high walls, and people gathered around it. The people of Uruk stood about it, all of them crowding in front, and the craftsmen pressed in behind. I laid it at your feet. I held it to me as I would hold a woman, so that you would count it as my equal.’

“The all-wise one, who knows all wisdom, answered her son; the all-wise one, who knows all wisdom, answered Gilgamesh: ‘The axe you saw is a man. You held him to your chest like a woman so that I would count him your equal. This is a brave heart, a friend, one who will stand by a comrade. His strength is the greatest in all the land; it is enormous, like the strength of Anu himself.’ Gilgamesh opened his mouth and said to his mother: ‘Whatever great danger comes, I shall have a friend.’ ”

chapters.title: Tablet II
paragraphs: While Gilgamesh was telling his dreams, Enkidu sat in front of the temple girl, and she bared her breasts and showed him her beauty, and the land of his birth slipped from his mind. For six days and seven nights Enkidu stayed with the courtesan, making love to her. Then the girl spoke up and said to Enkidu: “When I look at you, Enkidu, you seem godlike. Why wander the open country among the beasts? Come, I will take you to Uruk of the broad markets, to the holy temple, the home of Anu. Come, Enkidu, let me guide you to Eanna, the home of Anu, where Gilgamesh lives, the greatest of all creation. You will hold him in your arms like a woman and love him as you love yourself. Come, get up off the ground. That is only a shepherd’s bed.”

He heard what she said and took her advice; the woman’s words struck home in his heart. She took off one of her garments and dressed him in it, and she wore the other herself. Then, taking his hand as a sister takes a brother’s, she led him to the shepherds’ huts, the place of the sheepfolds. The shepherds gathered round when they saw him.

In the past he had been used to sucking the milk of wild animals! She set bread in front of him; he broke it, but he only gazed and stared. Enkidu did not know how to eat bread, and he had never learned how to drink beer! Then the woman spoke to Enkidu: “Enkidu, eat the bread; it is what life depends on. Drink the beer too; it is the custom of the land.” Enkidu ate the bread until he was full and drank seven cups of beer. His spirits rose and he was elated; his heart was glad and his face was bright. He rubbed himself down, oiled the hair of his body, and so he became human. He put on clothes to look like a man, took up his weapon and hunted the lions that preyed on the shepherds at night, and he caught the jackals. Now that he had mastered the lions, the shepherds slept soundly. Enkidu was their guard, a man in the full of his strength. Then one of the heroes spoke to Gilgamesh.

While he was taking his pleasure, he raised his eyes and noticed a man. He said to the woman: “Girl, bring that man here. What brings him here? I need to know his purpose.” The woman called the man over so that Enkidu could see him: “Sir, what are you looking for? Which way is your lodging?” The man spoke to Enkidu: “Gilgamesh is calling you to the meeting house of the community. This is the custom of men, and an honour paid to the great. Come and heap up the offerings that are owed to the city; come and bring in the city’s food for the common good. It is for the king of Uruk of the broad markets to receive your greeting, for Gilgamesh, king of Uruk of the broad markets, to receive your greeting. First he lies with the woman whom fate has allotted, and afterward he speaks by the counsel of the god, and from the shape of the omens he declares his destiny.” At the man’s words they went on ahead of him.

Enkidu walked in front and the courtesan came behind him. He entered Uruk of the broad markets, and the crowd gathered behind him. When he stopped in the street of Uruk of the broad markets, the people thronged behind him and cried: “He is the very image of Gilgamesh. He is a little shorter, but his build is stronger. Once he sucked the milk of wild animals like a helpless baby! The bread of Uruk always brings a man to the glory of his manhood! This mere savage has become a hero worth looking at. He is a match for godlike Gilgamesh.”

The bed is spread for the rites of love, and in the night Gilgamesh comes to sleep there and take his pleasure with the woman. But Enkidu comes out into the street, blocks the way in front of Gilgamesh, and threatens him with his strength.

Gilgamesh came on behind him. His rage flared up and he rushed to attack, and they met in the street. Enkidu blocked the door with his foot and would not let Gilgamesh in. They grappled and snorted like bulls, and they smashed the threshold. The very wall shook as Gilgamesh and Enkidu wrestled. They snorted like bulls, they smashed the threshold, and the very wall shook.

Gilgamesh bent his knee to the ground, and his fury died down; his rage was quelled. As soon as his rage had cooled, Enkidu said to Gilgamesh: “Truly your mother bore you to be one of a kind. Ninsun, the finest cow of the cattle pen, raised your head above all heroes, and Enlil has given you kingship over men.”

chapters.title: Tablet III
paragraphs: “He lifted his foot to the door. They raged at each other furiously. Enkidu has no equal; his hair is unkempt. He was born in the wild, and no one can stand against him.”

Enkidu stood and listened to what was said, and he sat down grieving, full of sorrow. His eyes filled with tears, his arms lost their strength, and the vigour drained out of his body. The two of them took each other by the hand and held on like brothers, and Enkidu answered Gilgamesh: “My friend, my love has put her arms around my neck to say goodbye. That is why my arms have lost their strength and the vigour has drained out of my body.”

Gilgamesh opened his mouth and said to Enkidu: “My friend, I have made up my mind to go to the Cedar Forest. I will overcome Humbaba the Fierce and destroy what is evil. Then I will cut down the cedar.”

Enkidu opened his mouth and said to Gilgamesh: “Listen, my friend. When I roamed the mountains with the herds, I used to go down into the depths of the forest, two hours’ march in from its edge. Humbaba: his roar is a whirlwind, there is fire in his jaws, and his very breath is death! Why have you set your heart on doing this? To meet Humbaba would be a fight beyond all others.” Gilgamesh opened his mouth and said to Enkidu: “I go to the forest because I need the rich yield of its mountains.”
Enkidu opened his mouth and said to Gilgamesh: “But when we go to the Cedar Forest, its guard is a fighter, strong and never sleeping, Gilgamesh.

“Enlil has appointed him to guard the Cedar Forest as a terror to mortals. Humbaba: his roar is a whirlwind, there is fire in his jaws, and his very breath is death! If he hears so much as a footstep on the road in his forest, he asks, ‘Who is this coming down into my forest?’ Enlil has appointed him to guard the Cedar Forest as a terror to mortals, and disaster will seize whoever comes down into his forest.”

Gilgamesh opened his mouth and said to Enkidu: “Who, my friend, is not conquered by death? A god, certainly, lives for ever in the daylight, but mortals have their days numbered, and everything they do is only wind. And here you are, afraid of death. Your courage gives you nothing solid. I will go in front of you! Your own mouth can tell how you feared the shock of battle. If I fall, I will have made my name last for ever: ‘It was Gilgamesh who fought Humbaba the Fierce!’ In the future, after children have been born in my house, they will climb onto your lap and say, ‘Tell us everything you know.’ When you talk like this you grieve my heart, because I have made up my mind to cut down the cedar and win fame that lasts for ever.

“Now, my friend, I want to give my orders to the craftsmen, so that they cast our weapons while we watch.” They gave their orders to the craftsmen. The workmen prepared the moulds and cast huge axes; they cast blades for the axes, each weighing three talents. They cast huge swords too, with hilts of two talents each and blades of thirty minas each to fit them, with inlay of thirty minas of gold for each sword. So Gilgamesh and Enkidu were each loaded with ten talents of weapons.

At the Gate of the Seven Bolts of Uruk the craftsmen heard the noise and gathered, and the people assembled in the streets of Uruk of the broad markets in Gilgamesh’s honour. The elders of Uruk of the broad markets took their seats in front of him, and Gilgamesh said: “Elders of Uruk of the broad markets, hear me! I am going against Humbaba the Fierce, who will say when he hears of it, ‘Let me have a look at this Gilgamesh people talk about, whose fame fills every country.’ I am the one who will overwhelm him there in the Cedar Forest. I will make the whole land hear how mighty the son of Uruk is, because I have made up my mind to cut down the cedars and win fame that lasts for ever.”

The elders of Uruk of the broad markets answered Gilgamesh: “Gilgamesh, you are young, and your courage carries you away. You do not fully know what you are trying to do. We have heard about Humbaba: he looks like two creatures in one. Who would willingly face his weapons in combat? Who would go down into the depths of the forest, two hours’ march in from its edge? Humbaba: his roar is a whirlwind, there is fire in his jaws, and his very breath is death! Why have you set your heart on doing this? To meet Humbaba would be a fight beyond all others.” Gilgamesh listened to his counsellors’ advice and thought it over. Then he called to his friend: “This, friend, is what I think. I am afraid of him, and yet I will go into the depths of the forest.”

“May your god protect you and bring you back safe and sound to the walls of Uruk of the broad markets.” Gilgamesh knelt before Shamash to speak to him: “Here I am, Shamash, lifting up my hands to you in prayer. Let my life be spared from now on. Bring me back to the ramparts of Uruk. Spread your protection over me.” And Shamash answered him, speaking his oracle.

Tears were streaming down Gilgamesh’s cheeks: “I am going on a road I have never travelled, by a way I do not know. But if I am spared, I will come back content and pay you the homage you are owed.” They brought the huge axes and put the bow and the quiver into his hand. He took an axe and slung on his quiver, took up another axe and fastened his sword to his belt. Before the two of them set out on their journey, they brought gifts to the Sun-god so that he would bring them home to Uruk safely.

Now the elders said goodbye to him with blessings and gave Gilgamesh advice about the road: “Gilgamesh, do not trust in your own strength alone. Let your road be scouted ahead of you, and guard yourself. Let Enkidu go in front of you. He is the one who has found the way and travelled that road. All the passes of the forest are under Humbaba’s rule, and the one who goes in front can protect his companion. May the Sun-god give you success in what you have set your heart on. May he let your eyes see the words of your mouth fulfilled. May he level the blocked path, cut a road for you to walk on, and split the mountain for your feet! May the god Lugalbanda send you a message in the night that will make you glad and help you in your purpose, for like a boy you have fixed your heart on overthrowing Humbaba, just as you decided. So wash your feet. When you stop to rest, dig a well, so that the water in your skin bottle is always pure, and pour cool water out to the Sun-god, and in this way you will remember Lugalbanda.”

Enkidu opened his mouth and said to Gilgamesh: “Gilgamesh, are you truly ready for this raid? Let your heart have no fear; put your trust in me.” He drew his cloak over his shoulder, and together they set out on the road to Humbaba. Along the way they met a man, who said: “They went with me, and I will tell you of it with joy in my heart.” When he heard what they had to say, the man set them on their way: “Go, Gilgamesh. Let your brother go in front of you in what you have set out to do. May the Sun-god grant you success!”

“Gilgamesh, do not put all your faith in the strength of your own body. Do not rely too much on your skill at striking. The one who goes in front can protect his companion; the one who knows the way has kept his friend safe. So let Enkidu go in front of you. He knows the road to the Cedar Forest. He is eager for battle and ready to fight. Enkidu will watch over a friend and protect a companion; a man like that will bring his comrade safely out of the pits. We, your council, have taken great care for your welfare, O King. In return, O King, you must take the same care for us.” Gilgamesh opened his mouth and said to Enkidu: “Come, my friend, let us go to the Palace of Splendour, into the presence of Ninsun, the glorious queen, to Ninsun, the wisest of all wise women, who knows everything. She will set out a well-planned road for our feet.”

Gilgamesh and Enkidu took each other by the hand and went to the Palace of Splendour. Gilgamesh came to the glorious queen, to Ninsun, and went into her presence: “Ninsun, I want to tell you that I am setting out on a long journey to Humbaba’s home, to face a kind of battle I do not know and follow a road I do not know, from the day I set out until I come back, until I reach the Cedar Forest, until I overthrow Humbaba the Fierce and wipe from the land every evil thing the Sun-god hates.”

“Dress yourself in your finery and come into the god’s presence.” Ninsun listened to her son, to Gilgamesh. She went into her room and adorned herself with tulal flowers. She put on the festival robe that suited her body, put on the festival jewel for her breast, and crowned her head with a circlet. She climbed the staircase, went up onto the roof and stood on the parapet. She offered incense to Shamash, made her sacrifice to Shamash, and then raised her hands toward Shamash and prayed: “Why did you give my son Gilgamesh this restless spirit? Now you have touched him and at once he sets out on a long journey to where Humbaba lives, to face a battle he does not know, to follow a road he does not know, from the day he sets out until he comes back, until he reaches the Cedar Forest, until he overthrows fierce Humbaba and wipes from the land every evil thing you hate. On the day you have fixed as the end of the journey of this strong man who fears you, may Aa your bride remind you of him. In the watches of the night he—”

“A man like that will bring his comrade safely out of the pits. We, your council, have taken great care for your welfare, O King. Now, O King, you must take the same care for us in turn.” Enkidu opened his mouth and said to Gilgamesh: “Turn back, my friend, from a road that is not—”

chapters.title: Tablet IV
paragraphs: Enkidu raised his eyes and spoke to the Gate as if it were a person: “Gate of the Forest, you have no understanding; you have no sense at all. For forty full leagues I have admired your wonderful timber, until I caught sight of the towering cedar. Your wood has no equal in the land. You are six gar high and two gar wide. Your post, your socket, your pivot, your lock and your shutter must all have been made for you in the city of Nippur! If only I had known, Gate, how grand you were and how beautifully you were built, I would have lifted an axe, or I would have bound you together.”

“Hurry, stand up to him; he will not chase you. We will go down into the wood together, and we will not be afraid. You shall put on seven garments, and putting on six more—” Like a mighty wild bull he flung the gate far away, and his mouth was full of his challenge. He shouted to the guard of the forest: “Get up! I am the one who will challenge Humbaba like a—”
“I see trouble ahead wherever I go. My friend, I have seen a dream that has not—” The day of the dream he had seen came true.

Enkidu lay sick for one day, then a second. Enkidu lay on his bed for a third day and a fourth, a fifth, sixth and seventh, an eighth, ninth and tenth. Enkidu lay in his sickness through the eleventh day and the twelfth; he was still lying on his bed. He called to Gilgamesh: “My comrade, someone hates me, because back in Uruk I was afraid of the fight. My friend, who in battle—”
Enkidu opened his mouth and said to Gilgamesh: “No, my friend, let us not go down into the depths of the forest at all. My hands have grown weak, and my arms are paralysed.”

Gilgamesh opened his mouth and said to Enkidu: “Shall we play the coward, my friend? You will outdo them all. My friend, you are skilled in war and shrewd in battle. So you will touch the—and you will have no fear of death.

“Let the paralysis that has struck your arms leave you, and let the weakness go out of your hands! Be brave and stand firm! My comrade, we will go down together. Do not let the fight weaken your courage in the least! Forget death and fear nothing. The man who is brave, cautious and careful has protected his own body by going in front, and he will protect his companion.” By their courage they would make a name for themselves. Then together they reached the barrier, and their talk fell silent, and they stopped short.

chapters.title: Tablet V
paragraphs: They stood still and stared at the forest. They gazed up at the height of the cedars and looked along the avenue into the forest. Where Humbaba walked there was a path; his tracks ran straight and the going was good. They also saw the Cedar Mountain, the home of the gods, the shrine of Irnini, where the cedar lifts its splendour against the mountainside. Its shade was lovely and full of delight, with bushes spreading out beneath it, and the cedar spread its fragrance.

“Then a second dream came to me, comrade, and this vision I saw was a pleasant one. The two of us were standing together high on a mountain peak, and then the peak toppled over and left the two of us like the creatures that are born in the wild.” Enkidu spoke to his comrade to explain the dream: “Comrade, this vision of yours promises us good fortune. You have seen a dream of great gain. Think, comrade: the mountain you saw must surely be Humbaba. This is what it means: we will capture Humbaba and throw down his body and leave his corpse in disgrace. I will show you tomorrow how it turns out.”

At the fortieth league they broke their fast with a mouthful of food. At the sixtieth they rested and dug a pit in the sunshine. Gilgamesh climbed up above it and poured out his flour as an offering for the mountain: “Mountain, grant me a dream. Breathe on him.” The mountain granted a dream and breathed on him. Then a cold blast of wind sprang up and a gust passed over, and it made him cower, and he swayed like the grain of the mountains. Gilgamesh squatted down with his knees bent and propped himself on his haunches, and at once sleep, the kind that flows over a man, came down on him. At midnight his sleep suddenly ended, and he hurried to speak to his comrade: “Did you not call me, my friend? Why have I woken up? Did you not touch me? Why am I afraid? Did some spirit pass by me? Why is my flesh all trembling?

“I have seen a third dream, comrade, and the dream I saw was terrifying. The sky roared, and the earth echoed back. The day went dark, blackness rose up, and lightning flashed. Flames flared up, and Plague was there too, filled to overflowing, and Death was gorged! Then the glare faded and the fires died down, and the falling embers turned to ash. Come, let us go down to the open country so that we can take counsel together.” Enkidu now spoke to Gilgamesh to explain his dream.

Another telling of the journey has the heroes stop for the night. At midnight sleep leaves Gilgamesh, and he asks, much as before, why he woke up afraid, and tells Enkidu his dream: “Besides my first dream I had a second. In my dream, my friend, a mountain threw me down and seized my feet. The brightness grew stronger, and there was a man, the most handsome in all the land. He pulled me out from under the mountain, gave me water to drink, and my heart was eased, and he set my feet back on the ground.” Enkidu spoke to Gilgamesh about this god: “My friend, we will go on, whatever stands against us. It is not the mountain. Come, put away your fear.”
And they cut off Humbaba’s head.

chapters.title: Tablet VI
paragraphs: Now he washed off the grime of battle and cleaned his tattered clothes. He braided his hair and let it fall loose over his shoulders. He threw off his dirty clothes and put on clean ones, put on armbands and fastened a sash around his body. Gilgamesh tied on his headband and girded himself with a sash.

Then the lady Ishtar caught sight of Gilgamesh’s beauty and said: “Come, Gilgamesh, be my bridegroom. Give me the gift of your body’s fruit. You will be my husband and I will be your wife. I will have a chariot made for you, all lapis blue and gold, with golden wheels and a yoke of precious stones, and every day great mules will be harnessed to it. Come into our house, fragrant with cedar. When you come into our house, threshold and throne will kiss your feet. Kings, princes and rulers will bow down before you and bring you the produce of mountain and plain as tribute. Your goats will bear in plenty, your ewes will have twins, your donkeys will grow as big as mules, the horses of your chariot will be famous for their gallop, and your mules under the yoke will never have a rival.”

Gilgamesh opened his mouth and answered the lady Ishtar: “Yes, but what would I have to give you if I took you as my wife? I would have to provide you with oil for your body and with clothes. I would have to give you your bread and your food, provisions fit for a goddess, and drink fit for a queen. I would be bound to you; we would pile up goods; I would dress you in robes. And what would I gain if I married you? You are nothing but a ruin that gives a man no shelter from the weather, a back door that keeps out neither gust nor gale, a palace that crushes the heroes inside it, a pit whose cover gives way under your feet, pitch that stains whoever carries it, a waterskin that leaks on whoever carries it, limestone that lets stone ramparts crumble into ruin, a charm of chalcedony that fails to protect you in enemy country, a sandal that trips up its owner on the road. Which husband did you ever love faithfully for all time? Which lord of yours ever got the better of you? Come, let me tell you the endless story of your husbands.

“You can vouch for the truth of this list yourself. Tammuz, the lover of your youth: year after year you make him the cause of weeping. Next you loved the brightly feathered roller bird, and yet you struck him and broke his wing. Now he stands in the grove crying ‘Kappi, my wing!’ You loved a lion too, in the full strength of his vigour, and yet you dug seven and seven deep pits to trap him. You loved a stallion too, magnificent in battle, and you brought him bridle, spur and whip. You made him gallop fifty miles, you brought him exhaustion and sweat, and after that you gave his mother Silili cause for deep mourning.

“You loved a shepherd too, a herdsman who never stopped heaping up the coals for you and every day slaughtered young lambs for you, and yet you struck him down and changed him into a jackal. His own herd boy chased him off, and the dogs he owned bit at his hindquarters.

“You loved Ishullanu too, your father’s gardener, who brought you delights without end and decked your table every day. You had only to cast your eyes on him to fall for him. ‘My Ishullanu, come, let me taste your strength. Reach out your hand.’ But Ishullanu said to you: ‘What are you asking of me? I have eaten nothing but what my mother baked, and what I would eat from you would be the bread of sin and wickedness! Besides, the reeds are cloak enough against the winter.’ When you heard his answer you struck him down and changed him into a spider, and made him live halfway up a wall, unable to move up for fear of the drip, or down for fear of being crushed. You would love me in my turn and then treat me just like them.”

When Ishtar heard this she flew into a rage and went up to heaven. Ishtar hurried to Anu her father and to Antu her mother and told them: “Father, Gilgamesh has heaped insults on me. Gilgamesh has been telling the story of my sins, my sins and wicked deeds.”

Anu opened his mouth and said to the lady Ishtar: “No, it was you who asked him to give you the gift of his body’s fruit. That is why he is telling the story of your sins, your sins and wicked deeds.”

Ishtar opened her mouth and said to Anu her father: “Father, make me a Bull of Heaven to defeat Gilgamesh, and fill its body with fire. But if you will not make me this Bull, then I will strike, I will set, I will—”

Anu opened his mouth and said to the lady Ishtar: “If I create the Bull of Heaven you are asking me for, seven years of empty husks will have to follow its attack. Will you gather grain for people and grow more fodder for the cattle?”

Ishtar opened her mouth and said to Anu her father: “I have stored up grain for people and grown fodder for the cattle. If seven years of empty husks must follow its attack, I will gather grain for people and grow more fodder for the cattle.”

Enkidu girded his waist, and at once Enkidu leapt, seized the Bull of Heaven by its horns, and threw the Bull of Heaven down full length in front of him, by the thick of its tail. Enkidu chased the Bull of Heaven, seized it, and held it by the thick of its tail.
When they had killed the Bull of Heaven, they tore out its heart and offered it in sacrifice to the Sun-god. When they had poured out their offering to the Sun, the two brothers sat down together.

Then Ishtar climbed onto the top of the ramparts of Uruk with its high walls. She went up onto the roof and there raised her wail: “Woe to Gilgamesh, who has killed the Bull of Heaven and made me mourn.” When Enkidu heard this, Ishtar’s shrieking, he tore the member out of the Bull and flung it in front of her: “If I could only have got my hands on you, I swear I would have done the same to you. I would have hung its guts around your waist like a belt.” Ishtar gathered the temple girls, the courtesans and the harlots, and over the member torn from the Bull she led the mourning.

Gilgamesh called the master craftsmen, the artists, every one of them, and all the craft guilds praised the size of the horns. Each horn had thirty minas of lapis blue for its setting, two fingers their— Together the two horns held six measures of oil. He dedicated them as an ointment offering to his god Lugalbanda, brought them in and hung them there in the shrine of his forefathers. Then they rinsed their hands in the Euphrates, set out and came back to the city. Now they strode along the main street of Uruk, and the heroes of Uruk thronged around to see them. Then Gilgamesh put a riddle to the leading men:
Tell me, who is the most splendid of heroes? Tell me, who is the most famous of giants? Gilgamesh is the most splendid of heroes. Enkidu is the most famous of giants.

So Gilgamesh held a great feast in his palace. Afterwards, while all the heroes lay asleep on their beds for the night, Enkidu too was asleep, and he saw a vision. Enkidu came to tell his dream and spoke to his comrade.

chapters.title: Tablet VII
paragraphs: “My friend, why are the great gods holding council together?”

Enkidu has dreamed that the gods took counsel together and decided that Enkidu must die and Gilgamesh must stay alive. Now Enkidu, struck down by fever, blames all his misfortune on the courtesan and heaps curses on her. The curse begins with the words “Destroy his power, weaken his strength,” spoken of Enkidu himself. Then, after some broken lines, Enkidu says: “The courtesan, who has brought a curse: courtesan, I will decree your fate for you, and your sorrows shall never end for all eternity. Come, I will curse you with a bitter curse. Desolation shall come on you with this curse. May your desire never be satisfied. May ruin fall on your house, may the street be your home, may the shade of the wall be where you live. May scorching heat and thirst strike down your strength.”
“Of want, since it is me she has— and the fever has laid me on my back.”

The Sun-god heard him, opened his mouth and called to him at once from heaven: “Enkidu, why are you cursing the courtesan? She was the one who gave you bread to eat, fit for a god, and wine to drink, fit for a king. She dressed you in a fine cloak and gave you splendid Gilgamesh as your companion. Now Gilgamesh, your friend and your brother, will lay you on a great bed. He will lay you to rest on a handsome bed and seat you on a throne of ease, a throne at his left hand, so that the princes of the underworld will kiss your feet. He will make all the people of Uruk weep for you and mourn you, and he will set girls and heroes to serve you. And for your sake he himself will let his body go unwashed, put on a lion’s skin and roam the open country.”
Enkidu listened to the words of valiant Shamash as he spoke, and his anger was calmed.

“May you be restored to your place! May kings, princes and chiefs fall in love with you. May no one slap his thigh in disgust at you. For you may the hero comb out his hair. May the man who wants to hold you undo his belt, and may your bed be lapis blue and gold. May he treat you kindly; may his ishshikku be heaped up for you. May the gods bring you in. May you be left the mother of seven brides.”

Enkidu, with misery in his belly, sleeping alone, came in the night to pour out his heaviness of heart to his comrade: “My friend, I saw a dream in the night. The sky roared and the earth echoed, and I was standing there alone. Then I saw a man whose face was dark, and his nails were like a lion’s claws. He overpowered me, climbed up on me, pressed me down, and on top of me my body—

“My hands were like a bird’s, and he seized me and led me to the House of Darkness, the home of Irkalla, to the house that no one who enters ever leaves! He led me by the road from which there is no coming back, to the house whose people live for ever without daylight, where dust is their food and mud their nourishment. They are dressed like birds in garments of feathers, and they sit in the darkness and never see the light. When I came to the gate, in that house the crown was brought low. As for those who wore crowns, who ruled the land in days of old, they were the ones who set out the baked meats for Anu and Enlil and served cool water from the waterskins. When I entered this House of Dust, there sat the high priest and the acolyte, the seer and the magician, the priest who anointed the great basin of the gods. Etana sat there, and Sumuqan; and the Queen of the Underworld too, Ereshkigal, before whom the scribe of the underworld, Belit-seri, kneels and reads aloud. She lifted her head and saw me, and took this—”

chapters.title: Tablet VIII
paragraphs: As soon as the first light of morning dawned, Gilgamesh spoke to Enkidu. He compared him to a gazelle and promised to give him glory. Then he recounted all they had done together: “We climbed the mountains and reached the Cedar Forest, travelling night and day, with wild beasts closing in behind us.” Enkidu lay dying, and then dead, and Gilgamesh wept over his friend before the elders of Uruk.

“Listen to me, elders, listen to me. I am weeping for my comrade Enkidu, crying bitterly like a woman who wails for the dead. My grip has gone slack on the axe at my side, and the sword in my belt is gone from my sight. My festival clothes give me no pleasure. Sorrow has attacked me and thrown me down in misery.

“My comrade and right hand, who hunted the wild donkey and the leopard of the open country, my comrade and right hand, who hunted the wild donkey and the leopard of the open country, Enkidu, together we overcame every danger and climbed the mountains. We captured the Bull of Heaven and destroyed it. We overthrew Humbaba, who lived in the Cedar Forest. What is this sleep that has come over you now? You have gone dark, and you cannot hear me.”

But he did not raise his eyes, and when Gilgamesh felt his heart, it was not beating. Then he covered his friend’s face like a bride’s. He raised his voice like a lion; he roared like a lioness robbed of her cubs. He paced back and forth in front of his comrade, tearing out his curls and throwing them down, plucking off and throwing away all his finery.

As soon as the first light of morning dawned, Gilgamesh spoke: “I, your friend and your brother, will lay you on a great bed. I will lay you to rest on a handsome bed and seat you on a great throne, a throne at my left hand, so that the princes of the underworld will kiss your feet. I will make all the people of Uruk weep for you and mourn you, and I will set girls and heroes to serve you. And for your sake I myself will let my body go unwashed, put on a lion’s skin and roam the open country.”
As soon as the first light of morning dawned, Gilgamesh loosened his belt.

“Judge of the Anunnaki.” When Gilgamesh heard this, he formed a picture of the slaying in his mind. Then at dawn Gilgamesh made a— and brought out a great platter of wood from the highlands. He filled a bowl of bright red stone with honey and a bowl of lapis blue with cream. He decorated the— and Shamash gave instruction.

chapters.title: Tablet IX
paragraphs: Gilgamesh wept bitterly for his comrade Enkidu as he roamed the open country: “Shall I not die too, just like Enkidu? Sorrow has come into my heart. I am afraid of death as I roam the open country. I will set out on the road to Utnapishtim, the son of Ubara-Tutu, and I will travel fast.

“If I reach the gates of the mountains in darkness and meet lions there, and terror falls on me, I will lift my head to the sky and pray to the Moon-god. Let my prayer reach the gods: ‘Save me!’ ” He slept, and saw a dream, and saw creatures rejoicing in life. He raised his axe in his hand, drew his sword from his belt, and leapt among them like a spear, striking and crushing.

The name of the hills was Mashu. He reached the mountains of Mashu, which keep watch every day over the rising and setting of the Sun-god. Their peaks reach up to the height of heaven, and their flanks reach down deep into the underworld. At their gates stand Scorpion-men on guard, terrible and frightening, whose very glance is death. Their splendour is overwhelming and shakes the hills. They are the wardens of Shamash at his rising and his setting. As soon as Gilgamesh saw them his face went pale with fear and dread, and he threw himself down in front of them, out of his senses.

Then the Scorpion-man said to his wife: “Look, the one coming toward us has a body made of the flesh of the gods.” His wife answered the Scorpion-man: “Two parts of him are god, and only a third of him is human.”

The Scorpion-man spoke to Gilgamesh, asked him why he had come on so far a journey, and told him how hard the crossing was. Gilgamesh told him that he meant to ask Utnapishtim about death and life. But the Scorpion-man said that no one had ever made that journey, that no one had ever crossed the mountains. The way through was the Road of the Sun, a journey of twenty-four hours that began in deep darkness. He described the journey to him hour by hour, and Gilgamesh accepted the test of his strength: “Even if it is in pain, even if my face is weathered by cold and heat, even if I go in grief, I will go.” Then the Scorpion-man, with a last word about the mountains of Mashu, said goodbye and wished him success. When Gilgamesh heard this, he set off at the Scorpion-man’s word and took the Road of the Sun. For the first two hours there was deep darkness and no light, and it did not let him see what lay behind him. Each two hours after that was the same until he had passed the eighth; at the ninth he came to the first glimmer of light. At last, at the twelfth double hour, he came out into the full blaze of the sun, and there he saw the Tree of the Gods.
Its fruit was all of red stone, and it was hung about with tendrils. It was lovely to look at. Its foliage was of lapis blue, and it bore fruit that delighted the eye.

“He has dressed himself in the skins of wild animals and eats their flesh. Gilgamesh, there will never be a crossing where there has never been one, not for as long as the wind drives the water.” Shamash was moved, and he called to Gilgamesh and spoke to him:

“Gilgamesh, why are you running, when you will not find the life you are looking for?” Gilgamesh answered the warrior Shamash: “After I have roamed up and down the wilderness as a wanderer, am I to lay my head in the depths of the earth and sleep there through all the years, for ever and ever? Let my eyes see the sun and be filled with its brightness. The darkness is driven far away when the brightness is wide. When will a dead man ever look on the light of the sun?”

chapters.title: Tablet X
paragraphs: There lived Siduri, the maker of wine. Wine was her trade. She was covered with a veil. Gilgamesh wandered toward her, dressed in animal skins. He had the flesh of the gods in his body, but there was misery in his belly, and his face was like the face of a man who has made a long journey. The wine-maker looked into the distance and said to herself, thinking it over in her heart: “This is a man who means harm to a woman. Where is he heading?” As soon as the wine-maker saw him, she barred her gate, barred her inner door, barred her room. At once Gilgamesh heard the sound of her shutting them, lifted his chin and turned his attention to her.
So Gilgamesh spoke to the wine-maker: “Wine-maker, what did you see, that you have barred your gate, barred your inner door and barred your room? I will strike down your door and break the bolt.”

The wine-maker answered Gilgamesh: “Why is your strength so wasted, why is your face so hollow? Why is your spirit full of sorrow, why has your cheerfulness gone? There is misery in your belly! Your face is like the face of a man who has made a long journey. Your face is weathered by cold and heat. Why must you roam the open country?” Gilgamesh answered the wine-maker: “Wine-maker, it is not that my strength is wasted or my face hollow, or that my spirit is full of sorrow or my cheerfulness gone. It is not misery in my belly, and it is not that my face is like the face of a man who has made a long journey, or that it is weathered by cold and heat, that I roam the open country like this.

“My comrade and right hand, who hunted the wild donkey and the leopard of the open country, my comrade and right hand, who hunted the wild donkey and the leopard of the open country, Enkidu: together we overcame every danger and climbed the mountains, captured the Bull of Heaven and destroyed it, overthrew Humbaba who lived in the Cedar Forest, and killed lions at the gates of the mountains. Enkidu shared every hardship with me. He was my comrade; together we killed the lions; he endured every hardship, and his fate has overtaken him. I mourned him for six days, for seven, until I could give him up for burial. Then I was afraid. I dreaded death, and so I roam the open country. What happened to my comrade weighs heavily on me. It is a long road I roam across the open country! What happened to Enkidu my comrade weighs heavily on me. It is a long road I roam across the open country. How can I keep silent? How can I speak? The comrade I loved so much has turned to dust. Enkidu, my comrade, the one I loved, has become like dust. Shall I not lie down like him too, and never come back for all eternity?”

“He who shared every hardship with me, whom I loved dearly, Enkidu, who shared every hardship with me, has perished. He has gone the way of all mankind! I have wept for him day and night, and I would not give him up to the tomb. But my friend does not come when I call. For six days, for seven, he lay on his face like a worm, and because of this I find no life, and must roam the open country like a hunter. So now, wine-maker, now that at last I see your face, let me not see the death I dread!”

The wine-maker answered Gilgamesh: “Gilgamesh, why are you running, when you cannot find the life you are looking for? When the gods first created mortals, they gave death to mankind and kept life in their own hands. Gilgamesh, keep your belly full. Be merry day and night, and make every day a holiday. Dance and rejoice day and night. Keep your clothes fresh, wash your head clean and bathe in the water. Care for the little one who holds your hand, and let your wife be happy in your arms. For this is what is given to man.”

Gilgamesh went on speaking to the wine-maker: “Tell me then, wine-maker, how do I get to Utnapishtim? What sign marks the way? Please give it to me, give me its sign. If it can be done, I will cross the ocean itself. If it cannot be done, I will roam the open country.”

The wine-maker answered Gilgamesh: “There has never been a crossing, Gilgamesh. No one who has come this far has ever been able to cross the ocean. Warrior Shamash crosses it, it is true, but who besides Shamash can make the crossing? The ferry is hard and its passage harder still, and the Waters of Death that bar the way to it are deep. Gilgamesh, even if you manage to cross the ocean, what will you do when you reach the Waters of Death? Gilgamesh, there is Urshanabi, Utnapishtim’s boatman. He has the sails, the urnu that he gathers in the forest. Let him see you now. If it can be done, cross with him. If it cannot, turn back and go home.”
When Gilgamesh heard this, he took his axe in his hand and drew his sword from his belt.

Then Urshanabi spoke to Gilgamesh: “Tell me your name. I am Urshanabi, the servant of Utnapishtim the Distant.” Gilgamesh answered him: “Gilgamesh is my name. I have come here from Uruk, from Eanna. I have crossed the mountains on the weary journey of the sunrise. Now that I have seen your face, Urshanabi, let me see Utnapishtim too, the Distant One!” Urshanabi answered Gilgamesh—
Then Urshanabi spoke to Gilgamesh, just as the wine-maker had: “Why is your strength so wasted?”

Gilgamesh went on speaking to Urshanabi: “Tell me, Urshanabi, how do I get to Utnapishtim? What sign marks the way? Please give it to me, give me its sign. If it can be done, I will cross the ocean itself. If it cannot be done, I will roam the open country.”

Urshanabi said to Gilgamesh: “Gilgamesh, it is your own hand that has kept you from crossing the ocean. You have destroyed the sails and broken the— Now the sails are destroyed, and the urnu are not— Gilgamesh, take your axe in your hand and go down to the forest. Cut poles five gar long, make knobs of bitumen for them and fit them with sockets, and bring them to me.”

When Gilgamesh heard this, he took the axe in his hand, drew the sword from his belt, went down to the forest and cut poles five gar long. He made knobs of bitumen, fitted them with sockets and carried them to Urshanabi. Then the two of them, Gilgamesh and Urshanabi, put out in their boat. They launched the boat on the waves and went aboard. On the third day, after a journey of a month and a half, he saw that Urshanabi had reached the Waters of Death.

Urshanabi said to Gilgamesh: “Gilgamesh, take it away. Do not let the Waters of Death touch your hand. Gilgamesh, take a second, a third and a fourth pole and push. Gilgamesh, take a fifth, a sixth and a seventh pole and push. Gilgamesh, take an eighth, a ninth and a tenth pole and push. Gilgamesh, take an eleventh, a twelfth pole!” With a hundred and twenty thrusts he had used up the poles. Then he undid his belt, and Gilgamesh set up the mast in its socket.

Utnapishtim looked into the distance, thinking it over in his heart, and said to himself: “Why are the sails of the boat destroyed? And why is someone who is not one of my own riding in the boat? This is no mortal coming here. I look, but this is no mortal. I look, and I look—”

Gilgamesh went on speaking to Utnapishtim: “Then I thought to myself, I will go and see what Utnapishtim the Distant has to say. So I came through every country, travelled over hard mountains and crossed every sea. My face has never had its fill of gentle sleep. I have worn myself out with hardship and loaded my flesh with sorrow. Before I reached the wine-maker’s house my clothes were worn out. Owl, bat, lion, leopard, wild cat, deer, ibex: I have eaten the flesh of them all, and dressed myself in their skins.”

“Do we build a house to last for ever? Do we seal a contract to last for ever? Do brothers go on sharing for ever? Does hatred last for ever among enemies? Does the river that has risen in flood bring its torrent for ever, the kulilu bird to the kirippu bird? The face that looks on the sunlight will soon be no more. The sleeper and the dead are alike. Death makes no distinction between servant and master once they have reached the span allotted to them. Then the Anunnaki, the great gods— Mammetum, the maker of destiny, settles destiny with them. They decide death and life, but the day of death is not revealed.”

chapters.title: Tablet XI
paragraphs: Gilgamesh said to Utnapishtim the Distant: “Utnapishtim, I look at you, and there is nothing strange about you. You are like me; you are no different at all. You are like me. A heart for fighting makes you complete, and yet you lie on your back at rest. Tell me, how did you come to stand in the assembly of the gods and ask for everlasting life?”

Utnapishtim answered Gilgamesh: “Gilgamesh, I will reveal to you the whole hidden story, and I will tell you the counsel of the gods. Shuruppak, a city you know well! It stands on the bank of the Euphrates. It is an old city, and the gods were in it. The great gods resolved to bring a flood. Anu their father was there; their adviser, warrior Enlil; Ninurta their herald; their leader Ennugi; and Ninigiku, who is Ea, sat in the plot with them.

“He gave away their plan to a reed hut: ‘Reed hut, reed hut! Wall, wall! Listen, reed hut! Think, wall. Mortal of Shuruppak, son of Ubara-Tutu, pull down your house and build a boat from it. Abandon your possessions and seek life. Let your treasure go and save life. Put every living creature aboard the boat. The boat you are to build must have the right proportions; let its width and its length match each other. Then launch it on the deep.’

“I understood, and I said to Ea my lord: ‘My lord, what you have told me I will honour and do. But what explanation am I to give the city, its people and its elders?’ Then Ea opened his mouth and said to me, his own servant!—‘Mortal, this is what you shall say to them: “Enlil hates me, and me alone, so that I may no longer live in your city or turn my face toward Enlil’s land. I will go down to the Deep and live there with Ea my lord. So he will shower plenty down on you, birds in great numbers and a catch of fish, and the harvest will be large. He will make plentiful rain come down on you.” ’

“As soon as the first light of morning dawned, the children brought pitch and the strong men brought everything that was needed. On the fifth day I laid out the shape of the boat. Its sides were each ten gar high, as planned, and its deck measured ten gar to match. I laid out the shape of the bow and built it. I cross-braced it six times, divided it into seven levels, and divided the inside into nine sections. I hammered in the caulking and found myself a punting pole, and added everything else that was needed. I smeared the hull with six shar of bitumen and three shar of pitch on the inside. Some people carried in a vessel of grease and brought me three shar of it; one shar of grease I left aside, which the rigging used up, and the boatman stowed away two shar. I slaughtered oxen, and every day I killed lambs. The workmen drank mead, beer, oil and wine as if they were water, and held a great feast like the New Year festival.

“Everything I owned I loaded aboard her. All the silver I owned I loaded, all the gold I owned I loaded aboard her, and all I owned of the seed of every living thing I loaded aboard her. I put all my kin and family on the boat with me, the cattle and the wild animals and all the craftsmen. Then Shamash fixed the hour: ‘He will send down a heavy rain in the night. Then go into the boat and shut your hatch at once.’ The appointed hour came, and in the night a heavy rain poured down. I looked at the face of the day, and the day was terrible to look at. So I went into the boat and shut my hatch at once, and to Puzur-Amurri the boatman, who sealed the boat, I handed over the stern and all its gear.

“As soon as the first light of dawn appeared, a black cloud rose up from the horizon, and Adad the storm-god was rumbling inside it. Nabu and Sharru went in front, coming as heralds over hill and plain. Then Irragal tore out the mooring posts. Ninurta came and let loose destruction. The Anunnaki raised their torches and scorched the land with their flames. The devastation of Adad reached up to heaven, and everything that was bright was turned to darkness.

“No brother could make out his brother, and from heaven no mortal could be seen. The gods were struck with terror at the Flood. They fled up to the heaven of Anu and crouched at its edges. The gods cowered like dogs, while Ishtar cried out like a woman in labour, the sweet-voiced lady of the gods shrieking aloud: ‘May that day turn to dust, because I spoke evil in the assembly of the gods! How could I speak such evil in the assembly of the gods, to wipe out my people and order destruction! Am I to give birth to my own people only for them to fill the sea like the spawn of fish?’

“The gods, the Anunnaki, wept with her. The gods sat humbled and weeping, and their lips were closed throughout the assembly. For six days and seven nights the hurricane, the flood and the storm went on sweeping over the land. On the seventh day the storm and the flood, which had fought like an army in battle, broke off their war. The sea grew calm, the gale was spent, the flood subsided. I looked at the day, and all sound had fallen silent. All mankind had returned to clay, and the swamp lay level with the rooftops.

“Then I opened a hatch, and the sunlight streamed down on my cheek. I bowed down and sat weeping, the tears running over my cheeks. I gazed into the distance, to the farthest edges of the ocean. Land rose up in twelve places, and the ark ran aground on Mount Nisir. Mount Nisir held it fast and would not let it move. One day, two days, Mount Nisir held it fast and would not let it move. Three days, four days, Mount Nisir held it fast and would not let it move. Five days, six days, Mount Nisir held it fast and would not let it move.

“When the seventh day dawned, I brought out a dove and let it go. The dove flew to and fro, but there was no place to rest, and it came back. Then I brought out a swallow and let it go. The swallow flew to and fro, but there was no place to rest, and it came back too. Then I brought out a raven and let it go. The raven flew off, saw that the waters had gone down, and ate as it waded and splashed about, and did not come back to me.

“I let everything go out to the four winds of heaven and offered a sacrifice. I poured out a drink offering on the top of the mountain. I set out seven and seven flagons and heaped sweet cane, cedar and myrtle beneath them. The gods smelled the savour, the gods smelled the sweet savour, and the gods gathered like flies around the one making the offering. Then the queen of the gods arrived and lifted up the magnificent jewels that Anu had made for her as she wished: ‘You gods! I would sooner forget this lapis necklace of mine than fail to keep these days in memory. I will never forget them. Let all the other gods come to the offering, but let Enlil alone not come to the offering, because without thinking he brought on the flood and gave my people up to be destroyed.’

“When Enlil arrived he caught sight of the boat, and at once Enlil flew into a rage, swollen with anger against the gods, the Igigi: ‘Has any mortal escaped? No man should have lived through that destruction.’ Then Ninurta spoke up and said to warrior Enlil: ‘Who but Ea could have devised such a plan? Ea knows every scheme.’

“Then Ea opened his mouth and said to warrior Enlil: ‘You, the chief of the gods, you warrior! How could you bring on a flood without taking counsel? Lay his sin on the sinner, lay his guilt on the guilty, but show mercy so that he is not cut off; be lenient so that he does not perish. Instead of making a flood, you could have let a lion come and thin out mankind. Instead of making a flood, you could have let a jackal come and thin out mankind. Instead of making a flood, you could have let a famine come and lay the land waste. Instead of making a flood, you could have let the Plague-god come and strike the people down. It was not I who revealed the secret of the great gods. I let the Exceedingly Wise one see a dream, and that is how he learned the secret of the gods. Now decide what is to be done with him.’

“Then Enlil came up into the ark. He took me by the hand and lifted me up, and he lifted my wife up too and made her kneel beside me. He stood between us, touched our foreheads and blessed us: ‘Until now Utnapishtim has been only a man. From now on Utnapishtim and his wife shall be like us gods. Utnapishtim shall dwell in the distance, where the rivers meet the sea.’ So they took me and settled me in the distance, where the rivers meet the sea. But as for you, who will call the gods together for your sake, so that you can find the life you are looking for? Come, do not sleep for six days and seven nights!”

But as he sat on his haunches, sleep blew over him like a breeze. Utnapishtim said to his wife: “Look at him, the strong man who wants life. Sleep has blown over him like a breeze!” His wife answered Utnapishtim the Distant: “Touch him and let the man wake up, so that he can go home in peace by the road he came, and go back to his land through the gate he left by.” Utnapishtim said to his wife: “How the troubles of mortals trouble you too! Bake his bread then and put it by his head, and mark on the wall of the house how long he sleeps.” She did so at once. She baked his bread, set it by his head, and marked on the house wall how long he slept. First his flour was gathered, second it was sifted, third it was moistened, fourth she kneaded his dough, fifth she added the leaven, sixth it was baked, and seventh, he touched him, and all of a sudden the great man woke up from his sleep!

Gilgamesh said to Utnapishtim the Distant: “Tell me, was it you who touched me all of a sudden, just as sleep was pouring over me, and woke me up?” Utnapishtim said to Gilgamesh: “Gilgamesh, your bread was counted out, and then I woke you. One: your flour was gathered. Two: it was sifted. Three: it was moistened. Four: she kneaded your dough. Five: she added the leaven. Six: it was baked. Seven: I touched you all of a sudden and you woke up.” Gilgamesh replied to the Distant One: “Utnapishtim, what am I to do, where am I to go? A robber has stolen my courage. Death lurks in my bedroom, and wherever I turn my ear, there is Death.”

Utnapishtim said to Urshanabi the boatman: “Urshanabi, the crossing will hate you. Its shore sets a limit to all who come to it. This man you guided here: must grime cover his body, must a skin hide the beauty of his limbs? Urshanabi, take him and lead him to where he can bathe, so that he can wash off his grime in water as white as snow. Let him throw off his skins and let the sea carry them away. Let his body look fair. Let the band round his head be renewed. Let him put on a cloak to cover his nakedness, and let the cloak show no sign of age but keep all its freshness until he reaches his city and finishes his journey.” So Urshanabi took him and led him to where he could bathe. He washed off his grime in water as white as snow and threw off his skins, so that the sea carried them away, and his body looked fair. He renewed the band round his head and dressed himself in a cloak to cover his nakedness, a cloak that would show no sign of age but keep all its freshness until he reached his city and finished his journey. Then Gilgamesh and Urshanabi went aboard their boat, launched it on the waves and set off in it.

Then Utnapishtim the Distant’s wife said to him: “Gilgamesh came here worn out with rowing. What will you give him to take back to his land?” Meanwhile Gilgamesh had raised his pole and was pushing the boat toward the shore. Utnapishtim spoke to Gilgamesh: “Gilgamesh, you came here worn out with rowing. What shall I give you to take back to your country? Gilgamesh, I will reveal to you a hidden thing; I will tell you. There is a plant like a thorn, with its root deep down in the ocean. Its prickles will scratch you like a briar’s, but if your hand reaches that plant, you will surely find everlasting life.” When Gilgamesh heard this, he loosened the belt around him and tied heavy stones to his feet, and they dragged him down into the depths of the sea. He found the plant, and as he seized it, its prickles scratched him. He cut the heavy stones from his feet so that the sea would carry him back to its shore.

Gilgamesh said to Urshanabi the boatman: “Urshanabi, this is a wondrous plant,” he said. “By it a man can gain his heart’s desire. I will take it to Uruk with its high walls and give it to— to eat. Its name is ‘The Old Man Becomes a Young Man Again’, and I will eat it myself, so that I can return to the state of my youth.”

At the fortieth hour they broke their fast; at the sixtieth they rested. Gilgamesh saw a pool of cool water, went down into it and bathed. But there was a snake, which smelled the fragrance of the plant. It darted up out of the water and snatched the plant, uttering a curse as it drew back. Then Gilgamesh sat down and burst into tears. The tears ran down his cheeks, and he said to Urshanabi the boatman: “Tell me, Urshanabi, for whom have my arms laboured? For whom has my heart’s blood been spent? I have not won the prize for myself. I have won it only for the lion of the earth, and now, at the fortieth hour, such a creature has stolen it. When I opened the sluice and loosed the gear, I saw the sign that was given to me as a warning. If only I had turned back and left the boat at the shore!” At the fortieth hour they broke their fast; at the sixtieth they rested; and at last they arrived in the middle of Uruk with its high walls.

Gilgamesh said to Urshanabi the boatman: “Urshanabi, go up and walk on the ramparts of Uruk. Look at its foundation and study its brickwork. Are its bricks not baked in the kiln, and is its groundwork not laid in bitumen, seven courses deep? One shar is city, one shar is gardens, and one shar is— with the temple of Ishtar, three shar I have gathered together, and the— of Uruk.”

chapters.title: Tablet XII
paragraphs: Then, when the dragnet had passed through the Architect’s house and the net had taken its toll, he said: “Lord, what can I do, now that the dragnet has passed through the Architect’s house and the net has taken its toll?” Gilgamesh said to him: “If to—”

“Gilgamesh—” “If you go to the temple, you must not put on clean clothes; go like an ordinary townsman. You must not anoint yourself with sweet oil from the flask, or the dead will gather round you at its fragrance. You must not set a bow on the ground, or those killed by the bow will circle round you. You must not carry a stick in your hand, or the stricken ghosts will gibber at you. You must not put shoes on your feet or make a loud echo on the ground. You must not kiss the wife you love or strike the wife you hate. You must not kiss the child you love or strike the child you hate, for the mourning of the earth holds you in its grip.
“She who lies dead, she who lies dead, the mother of Ninazu, she who lies dead: her fair shoulders are no longer veiled with a cloak, her breast no longer full like the flask of fat!”

So he went to the temple. He put on clean clothes and went like an ordinary townsman. He anointed himself with sweet oil from the flask, and at its fragrance the dead gathered round him. He set his bow on the ground, and the spirits circled round him; those killed by the bow gibbered at him. He carried a stick in his hand, and the stricken ghosts gibbered at him. He put shoes on his feet and made a loud echo on the ground. He kissed the wife he loved and beat the wife he hated; the child he loved he kissed, and the child he hated he beat. Truly the mourning of the earth held him in its grip:
“She who lies dead, she who lies dead, the mother of Ninazu, she who lies dead: her fair shoulders are no longer veiled with a cloak, her breast no longer full like the flask of fat.”

He cried out for Enkidu to come up out of the earth: “It was not Namtar, the Plague-god, who seized him, nor fever, but only the earth. It was not Nergal the Croucher, the ruthless one, who seized him, but only the earth. He did not fall where mortals do battle. It was only the earth that seized him.” So the son of Ninsun grieved for Enkidu his servant,

and he went all alone to Ekur, the temple of Enlil: “Enlil, my father, now the dragnet has struck me too, struck me down to the earth; the net has struck me to the earth as well. It is Enkidu, whom I beg you to raise up from the earth. It was not Namtar, the Plague-god, who seized him, nor fever, but only the earth. It was not Nergal the Croucher, the ruthless one, who seized him, but only the earth. He did not fall where mortals do battle. It was only the earth that seized him.” But Enlil the father gave no answer.

He hurried to the Moon-god: “Moon-god, my father, now the dragnet has struck me too, struck me down to the earth; the net has struck me to the earth as well. It is Enkidu, whom I beg you to raise up from the earth. It was not Namtar, the Plague-god, who seized him, nor fever, but only the earth. It was not Nergal the Croucher, the ruthless one, who seized him, but only the earth. He did not fall where mortals do battle. It was only the earth that seized him.” But the Moon-god gave no answer.

Then he hurried to Ea: “Ea, my father, now the dragnet has struck me too, struck me down to the earth; the net has struck me to the earth as well. It is Enkidu, whom I beg you to raise up from the earth. It was not Namtar, the Plague-god, who seized him, nor fever, but only the earth. It was not Nergal the Croucher, the ruthless one, who seized him, but only the earth. He did not fall where mortals do battle. It was only the earth that seized him.”

Ea the father listened, and he said to Nergal the warrior hero: “Nergal, warrior hero, listen to what I say! Open a hole in the earth now, so that the spirit of Enkidu can rise up out of the earth and speak with his brother.” Nergal the warrior hero listened to what Ea said.

He opened a hole in the earth, and the spirit of Enkidu came up out of the earth like a wind. They embraced and spoke together, mourning. “Tell me, my friend, tell me, my friend, please tell me what you have seen of the laws of the underworld.” “No, comrade, I will not tell you, I will not tell you. If I were to tell you what I have seen of the laws of the underworld, you would sit down and weep!” “Then let me sit down and weep.”

“So be it. The friend you held close, who made your heart glad: the worm has gone into his body as into an old cloak. The bride you held close, who made your heart glad: her body is filled with dust. He has spoken, and he has sunk into the ground; he has spoken, and he has sunk into the ground.”
“The one who fell in— did you see him?” “Yes, I saw him.” “Like a beautiful pillar he holds up an inner porch.”

“The one who fell from a pole, did you see him?” “Yes, I saw him. At once, by pulling out a peg—” “The one whom death took, did you see him?” “Yes, I saw him. He rests on a bed and drinks clear water.” “The hero killed in battle, did you see him?” “Yes, I saw him. His father and mother hold up his head, and his wife bends over him in bitter grief.”

“The one whose body lies in the open country, have you seen him?” “Yes, I saw him. His spirit does not rest in the earth.” “The one whose ghost has no one to care for it, did you see him?” “Yes, I saw him. What he eats is the leftovers in the cup and the crusts of bread tossed into the street.”
